### Prerequisites

text.text:
### Writing integer numbers on the abacus

Recognizing the importance of practice exercises as a way to reinforce knowledge (<htcite0>), we present below a game that uses the same abacus board as the previous practices. The game draws a random integer number, and the task is to represent it on the abacus bead by bead — while the game teaches, step by step, how the number is written.

#### How the game works

When the page loads, the abacus is initialized with the first level and a random integer number is drawn. The decimal point (⚫) stays at the rightmost column: the column where it sits is the units, and the columns to its left are the other integer families (tens, hundreds, thousands and so on, up to the last column of the board). There are no fractional columns in this game.

Follow the instructions between the level badge and the "➡️ Next step" button: each one asks you to write a single digit in one column. When you complete the step correctly, the message "✅ Correct! Click 'Next step' to continue." appears at the bottom of the abacus. After the last digit, a final step asks you to check the whole number.

When you complete the calculation, you receive: "🎉🎉🎉 PERFECT! 🎉🎉🎉". You can repeat as many numbers as you want at the same level with "🎲 New number", and you can advance to the next level with "⭐ Next level".

#### The nine levels

The game starts with numbers like **x**: one digit in the units column. Then a level is added for each integer family: **xx** (tens), **xxx** (hundreds), **xxxx** (thousands), **xxxxx** (ten thousands), **xxxxxx** (hundred thousands), **xxxxxxx** (millions), **xxxxxxxx** (ten millions) and **xxxxxxxxx** (hundred millions), the last available column. All levels use only integer numbers: the decimal point (⚫) always rests on the rightmost column, so the game never asks you to move it or to write a decimal digit.

source.text: Costa, M., Cardoso, A. P., Lacerda, C., Lopes, A., & Gomes, C.
